questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -5 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of $A$ is $|A| = (1)(4) - (-5)(-2) = 4 - 10 = -6$

The adjoint of $A$ is obtained by interchanging the diagonal elements and changing the signs of the off-diagonal elements:

$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

The inverse of the matrix is given by $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$

$A^{-1} = -\dfrac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 1 & b \end{bmatrix}$, where $a$ and $b$ are the roots of the equation $x^2 - 4x + 2 = 0$. If $A + A^{-1} = kI_2$, then the value of $k$ is ____
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 1 & b \end{bmatrix}$

Since $a$ and $b$ are roots of $x^2 - 4x + 2 = 0$, we have $a + b = 4$ and $ab = 2$.

The determinant of $A$ is $|A| = ab - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1$.

The inverse of $A$ is $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \begin{bmatrix} b & -1 \\ -1 & a \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} b & -1 \\ -1 & a \end{bmatrix}$.

Now, $A + A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ 1 & b \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} b & -1 \\ -1 & a \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a+b & 0 \\ 0 & a+b \end{bmatrix}$.

Substituting $a + b = 4$, we get $A + A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = 4I_2$.

Comparing with $A + A^{-1} = kI_2$, we get $k = 4$.

questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ such that $XA = B^T$ and $A^{-1}Y = B$, then $XY = $
questions.solution:
Given $XA = B^T$

Post-multiplying by $A^{-1}$, we get $X = B^T A^{-1}$

Given $A^{-1}Y = B$

Pre-multiplying by $A$, we get $Y = AB$

Now, $XY = (B^T A^{-1})(AB)$

Using the associative property of matrix multiplication, $XY = B^T (A^{-1}A) B$

$XY = B^T I B = B^T B$

Substituting the given matrix $B$, we get:

$XY = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$

$XY = [1 \times 1 + 0 \times 0 + 1 \times 1] = [2]$

Answer: $[2]$

questions.q: The inverse of the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 4 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is $B = \dfrac{1}{37}\begin{bmatrix} -5 & 9 & 11 \\ -3 & -2 & 14 \\ 11 & -5 & k \end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $k$ is...
questions.solution:
Since $B$ is the inverse of $A$, we have $AB = I$, which implies $A(37B) = 37I$.

The element in the first row and third column of the matrix $37I$ is $0$.

Multiplying the first row of $A$ with the third column of $37B$, we get:

$2(11) + (-1)(14) + 4(k) = 0$

$22 - 14 + 4k = 0$

$8 + 4k = 0$

$k = -2$

Alternatively, multiplying the third row of $A$ with the third column of $37B$ gives the element in the third row and third column of $37I$, which is $37$:

$1(11) + 2(14) + 1(k) = 37$

$11 + 28 + k = 37$

$39 + k = 37$

$k = -2$

Answer: $-2$

questions.q: If matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2025 & 2026 \\ 0 & 2 & 2027 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, then the sum of all elements in $\text{adj}(A^{-1})$ is equal to...
questions.solution:
For any invertible matrix $M$, we have the property $\text{adj}(M) = |M| M^{-1}$.

Substituting $M = A^{-1}$, we get:

$\text{adj}(A^{-1}) = |A^{-1}| (A^{-1})^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} A$

Since $A$ is an upper triangular matrix, its determinant is the product of its diagonal elements:

$|A| = (-1) \times 2 \times (-1) = 2$

Thus, $\text{adj}(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{2} A$.

The sum of all elements in $\text{adj}(A^{-1})$ will be $\dfrac{1}{2}$ times the sum of all elements in $A$.

Sum of all elements in $A = -1 + 2025 + 2026 + 0 + 2 + 2027 + 0 + 0 + (-1)$

Sum $= 2025 + 2026 + 2027 = 6078$

Therefore, the sum of all elements in $\text{adj}(A^{-1})$ is:

$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6078 = 3039$

questions.q: The inverse of matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1+pq & p & 0 \\ q & 1+pq & p \\ 0 & q & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is ...
options: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & p & p^2 \\ q & 1+pq & p+p^2q \\ q^2 & q+pq^2 & 1+pq+p^2q^2 \end{bmatrix}$
questions.solution:
Let the given matrix be $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1+pq & p & 0 \\ q & 1+pq & p \\ 0 & q & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

The inverse of matrix $A$ is given by $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\text{adj}(A)$.

First, evaluate the determinant of $A$:

$|A| = (1+pq)[(1+pq)(1) - (p)(q)] - p[q(1) - (p)(0)] + 0$

$|A| = (1+pq)[1 + pq - pq] - p[q]$

$|A| = (1+pq)(1) - pq = 1 + pq - pq = 1$

Since $|A| = 1$, the inverse matrix is $A^{-1} = \text{adj}(A)$.

To find the adjoint of $A$, we calculate the cofactors of each element:

$C_{11} = (1+pq)(1) - pq = 1$

$C_{12} = -(q(1) - 0) = -q$

$C_{13} = q(q) - 0 = q^2$

$C_{21} = -(p(1) - 0) = -p$

$C_{22} = (1+pq)(1) - 0 = 1+pq$

$C_{23} = -((1+pq)q - 0) = -(q + pq^2)$

$C_{31} = p(p) - 0 = p^2$

$C_{32} = -((1+pq)p - 0) = -(p + p^2q)$

$C_{33} = (1+pq)^2 - pq = 1 + 2pq + p^2q^2 - pq = 1 + pq + p^2q^2$

The adjoint matrix is the transpose of the cofactor matrix:

$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} C_{11} & C_{21} & C_{31} \\ C_{12} & C_{22} & C_{32} \\ C_{13} & C_{23} & C_{33} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -p & p^2 \\ -q & 1+pq & -(p+p^2q) \\ q^2 & -(q+pq^2) & 1+pq+p^2q^2 \end{bmatrix}$

Therefore, $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -p & p^2 \\ -q & 1+pq & -(p+p^2q) \\ q^2 & -(q+pq^2) & 1+pq+p^2q^2 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.q: If $A = [a_{ij}]_{3\times3}$, where $a_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } i+j \text{ is even} \\ 0, & \text{if } i+j \text{ is odd} \end{cases}$, then $\text{adj}(A) = \ldots$ ..
questions.solution:
Given $A = [a_{ij}]_{3\times3}$ where $a_{ij} = 1$ if $i+j$ is even, and $0$ if $i+j$ is odd.

Constructing the matrix $A$:

$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

The adjoint of $A$ is the transpose of the cofactor matrix $C$. Calculating the cofactors $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$:

$C_{11} = 1, C_{12} = 0, C_{13} = -1$

$C_{21} = 0, C_{22} = 0, C_{23} = 0$

$C_{31} = -1, C_{32} = 0, C_{33} = 1$

The cofactor matrix is $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Taking the transpose of $C$ gives the adjoint matrix:

$\text{adj}(A) = C^T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and if $A^2 - 2A + I = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & p \\ q & 11 \end{bmatrix}$, then $\ldots$
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

First, we calculate $A^2$:
$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 + 2 & -6 + 8 \\ -3 + 4 & 2 + 16 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 2 \\ 1 & 18 \end{bmatrix}$

Next, we calculate $2A$:
$2A = 2 \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 4 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, substituting these into $A^2 - 2A + I$:
$A^2 - 2A + I = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 2 \\ 1 & 18 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 4 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

$= \begin{bmatrix} 11 - (-6) + 1 & 2 - 4 + 0 \\ 1 - 2 + 0 & 18 - 8 + 1 \end{bmatrix}$

$= \begin{bmatrix} 18 & -2 \\ -1 & 11 \end{bmatrix}$

We are given that $A^2 - 2A + I = \begin{bmatrix} 18 & p \\ q & 11 \end{bmatrix}$.

Comparing the corresponding elements of the matrices, we get:
$p = -2$
$q = -1$

Answer: $p = -2,\ q = -1$

questions.q: If matrix A and its inverse $A^{-1}$ are given by $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & x & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} & -\dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} \\ -4 & 3 & y \\ \dfrac{5}{2} & -\dfrac{3}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}$, then the polar co-ordinates of the points whose Cartesian co-ordinates are $(x, y)$ are $\ldots$
questions.solution:
Since $A A^{-1} = I$, the product of the first row of $A$ and the third column of $A^{-1}$ must be $0$.

$0 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 \times y + 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow y + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1$

Similarly, the product of the third row of $A$ and the first column of $A^{-1}$ must be $0$.

$3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + x \times (-4) + 1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow 4 - 4x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1$

The Cartesian coordinates are $(x, y) = (1, -1)$.

The polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ are given by $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ and $\tan \theta = \dfrac{y}{x}$.

$r = \sqrt{1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{2}$

Since the point $(1, -1)$ lies in the fourth quadrant, $\theta = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}$.

Thus, the polar coordinates are $\left(\sqrt{2}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right)$.

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -13 \\ 5 & -10 \end{bmatrix}$ be two matrices. If the variables $x$ and $y$ satisfy the matrix equation $((A^{-1})^2 + B)\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$, then the ordered pair $(x, y) = $
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

Determinant of $A$ is $|A| = (3)(-1) - (-4)(1) = 1$

The inverse of $A$ is $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, $(A^{-1})^2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 4 & -4 + 12 \\ 1 - 3 & -4 + 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$

Adding matrix $B$:

$(A^{-1})^2 + B = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 8 \\ -2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -13 \\ 5 & -10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 3 & -5 \end{bmatrix}$

The given matrix equation is $((A^{-1})^2 + B)\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$

$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ 3 & -5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$

This gives the equation $3x - 5y = 0 \Rightarrow 3x = 5y$

Checking the given options, the ordered pair $(5, 3)$ satisfies this equation since $3(5) - 5(3) = 0$.

Answer: $(5, 3)$

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & -\sin\alpha & 0 \\ \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. If $B = \text{adj}\,A$, then the matrix $B^{-1}$ is equal to...
questions.solution:
The determinant of matrix $A$ is given by

$|A| = \cos\alpha(\cos\alpha - 0) - (-\sin\alpha)(\sin\alpha - 0) + 0$

$|A| = \cos^2\alpha + \sin^2\alpha = 1$

We know the property of adjoint of a matrix:

$A(\text{adj}\,A) = |A|I$

Substituting $|A| = 1$, we get

$A(\text{adj}\,A) = I$

$\Rightarrow \text{adj}\,A = A^{-1}$

It is given that $B = \text{adj}\,A$, so

$B = A^{-1}$

Taking the inverse on both sides, we obtain

$B^{-1} = (A^{-1})^{-1} = A$

Answer: $A$

questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$; $B = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ then, $(2A + 3B)^{-1} =$ _______
questions.solution:
$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$

$B = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

$2A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 14 \end{bmatrix}$

$3B = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$

$2A + 3B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 + 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 14 + 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 26 \end{bmatrix}$

The inverse of a diagonal matrix is obtained by taking the reciprocal of its diagonal elements.

$(2A + 3B)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\dfrac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{26} \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\dfrac{1}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{26} \end{bmatrix}$

questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} \\ \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} \\ -\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ then $A^{-1}B$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $t = \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}$.

The given matrices can be written as:
$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -t \\ t & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of $A$ is $|A| = 1(1) - (-t)(t) = 1 + t^2$.

The adjugate of $A$ is $\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Therefore, the inverse of $A$ is:
$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A) = \dfrac{1}{1+t^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, multiply $A^{-1}$ and $B$:
$A^{-1}B = \dfrac{1}{1+t^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

$A^{-1}B = \dfrac{1}{1+t^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1(1) + t(-t) & 1(t) + t(1) \\ -t(1) + 1(-t) & -t(t) + 1(1) \end{bmatrix}$

$A^{-1}B = \dfrac{1}{1+t^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 - t^2 & 2t \\ -2t & 1 - t^2 \end{bmatrix}$

$A^{-1}B = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2} & \dfrac{2t}{1+t^2} \\ \dfrac{-2t}{1+t^2} & \dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2} \end{bmatrix}$

Using the half-angle trigonometric identities $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1 - \tan^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}}{1 + \tan^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}}$ and $\sin\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}}{1 + \tan^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}}$, we get:

$A^{-1}B = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$

questions.q: If $A$ is a non-singular matrix and $A^2 - A + I = 0$, then $A^{-1} = \ldots$
questions.solution:
Given $A^2 - A + I = 0$

Multiplying both sides by $A^{-1}$, we get

$A^{-1}(A^2 - A + I) = 0$

$A - I + A^{-1} = 0$

$A^{-1} = I - A$

Answer: $I - A$

questions.q: If the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ is expressed as the sum of a symmetric matrix B and a skew symmetric matrix C then which of the following relations is correct?
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

The transpose of matrix $A$ is $A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

Any square matrix can be expressed as the sum of a symmetric matrix $B$ and a skew-symmetric matrix $C$, where $B = \dfrac{1}{2}(A + A^T)$ and $C = \dfrac{1}{2}(A - A^T)$

$B = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

$C = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \right) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

Calculating the determinants of $A$, $B$, and $C$:

$|A| = (4)(2) - (1)(3) = 5$

$|B| = (4)(2) - (2)(2) = 4$

$|C| = (0)(0) - (-1)(1) = 1$

Checking the given relations, we find that $|B| + |C| = 4 + 1 = 5$

Therefore, $|A| = |B| + |C|$

Answer: $|A| = |B| + |C|$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A^2 + xA + yI_2 = O_2$, where $I_2$ and $O_2$ are the identity matrix and null matrix of order 2 respectively, then:
questions.solution:
$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

Substituting $A^2$, $A$, and $I_2$ into the given equation $A^2 + xA + yI_2 = O_2$:

$\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + x \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

$\begin{bmatrix} 4 + 2x + y & -4 - x \\ 0 & 4 + 2x + y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

Equating the corresponding elements to zero:

$-4 - x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -4$

$4 + 2x + y = 0$

Substituting $x = -4$ into the second equation:

$4 + 2(-4) + y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 4$

Answer: $x = -4,\ y = 4$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = [a_{ij}]_{3 \times 3}$ is a matrix such that $a_{ij} = |2i - 5j|$, where $|.|$ denotes the modulus function, then the element in the $2^{\text{nd}}$ row and $3^{\text{rd}}$ column of $A^{-1}$ is ...
questions.solution:
Given $a_{ij} = |2i - 5j|$, we construct the matrix $A$ of order $3 \times 3$:

$A = \begin{bmatrix} |2(1)-5(1)| & |2(1)-5(2)| & |2(1)-5(3)| \\ |2(2)-5(1)| & |2(2)-5(2)| & |2(2)-5(3)| \\ |2(3)-5(1)| & |2(3)-5(2)| & |2(3)-5(3)| \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 8 & 13 \\ 1 & 6 & 11 \\ 1 & 4 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of matrix $A$ is:

$|A| = 3(54 - 44) - 8(9 - 11) + 13(4 - 6)$

$|A| = 3(10) - 8(-2) + 13(-2) = 30 + 16 - 26 = 20$

The element in the $2^{\text{nd}}$ row and $3^{\text{rd}}$ column of $A^{-1}$ is given by $\dfrac{C_{32}}{|A|}$, where $C_{32}$ is the cofactor of the element $a_{32}$ in matrix $A$.

Calculating the cofactor $C_{32}$:

$C_{32} = (-1)^{3+2} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 13 \\ 1 & 11 \end{vmatrix} = -(33 - 13) = -20$

Therefore, the required element is:

$\dfrac{C_{32}}{|A|} = \dfrac{-20}{20} = -1$

Answer: $-1$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, $B^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{2}{5} & -\dfrac{1}{5} \end{bmatrix}$, then $(AB)^{-1} = $
questions.solution:
Using the reversal law for the inverse of a product of matrices, we have:

$(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$

First, we find the inverse of matrix $A$. The determinant of $A$ is:

$|A| = (2)(-2) - (3)(5) = -4 - 15 = -19$

The adjugate of $A$ is obtained by swapping the diagonal elements and changing the signs of the off-diagonal elements:

$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

Thus, $A^{-1}$ is given by:

$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A) = \dfrac{1}{-19} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{19} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$

We are given $B^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5} \\ \dfrac{2}{5} & -\dfrac{1}{5} \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Now, we compute $(AB)^{-1}$ by multiplying $B^{-1}$ and $A^{-1}$:

$(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} = \left( \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \right) \left( \dfrac{1}{19} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \right)$

$(AB)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{95} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$

Performing the matrix multiplication:

$(AB)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{95} \begin{bmatrix} (1)(2) + (2)(5) & (1)(3) + (2)(-2) \\ (2)(2) + (-1)(5) & (2)(3) + (-1)(-2) \end{bmatrix}$

$(AB)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{95} \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 10 & 3 - 4 \\ 4 - 5 & 6 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{95} \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -1 \\ -1 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{95}\begin{bmatrix} 12 & -1 \\ -1 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5a & -b \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $A\,(\text{adj }A) = AA^T$, Then $5a + b =$
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5a & -b \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

Using the property $A(\text{adj } A) = |A|I$, the given equation becomes $AA^T = |A|I$.

$|A| = (5a)(2) - (-b)(3) = 10a + 3b$

$AA^T = \begin{bmatrix} 5a & -b \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5a & 3 \\ -b & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 25a^2 + b^2 & 15a - 2b \\ 15a - 2b & 13 \end{bmatrix}$

Equating $AA^T$ to $|A|I$:

$\begin{bmatrix} 25a^2 + b^2 & 15a - 2b \\ 15a - 2b & 13 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10a + 3b & 0 \\ 0 & 10a + 3b \end{bmatrix}$

From the off-diagonal elements:

$15a - 2b = 0 \Rightarrow b = \dfrac{15a}{2}$

From the bottom-right elements:

$10a + 3b = 13$

Substituting $b = \dfrac{15a}{2}$ into the equation:

$10a + 3\left(\dfrac{15a}{2}\right) = 13$

$\dfrac{20a + 45a}{2} = 13$

$\dfrac{65a}{2} = 13 \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{26}{65} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

Substituting $a = \dfrac{2}{5}$ to find $b$:

$b = \dfrac{15}{2} \left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right) = 3$

$5a + b = 5\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right) + 3 = 2 + 3 = 5$

Answer: $5$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Inverse of $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of $A$ is $|A| = (3)(4) - (-2)(1) = 12 + 2 = 14$

The adjugate of $A$ is $\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$

The inverse of $A$ is given by $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$

$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{14} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{14} & \dfrac{2}{14} \\ -\dfrac{1}{14} & \dfrac{3}{14} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{7} & \dfrac{1}{7} \\ -\dfrac{1}{14} & \dfrac{3}{14} \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{7} & \dfrac{1}{7} \\ -\dfrac{1}{14} & \dfrac{3}{14} \end{bmatrix}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The element in the third row and the second column in the inverse matrix of a matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ is
questions.solution:
Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

The element in the third row and second column of $A^{-1}$ is given by $\dfrac{C_{23}}{|A|}$, where $C_{23}$ is the cofactor of the element $a_{23}$ in $A$.

First, we calculate the determinant of $A$:

$|A| = 1(1 \times 4 - 3 \times 3) - 3(3 \times 4 - 3 \times 3) + 3(3 \times 3 - 1 \times 3)$

$|A| = 1(-5) - 3(3) + 3(6) = -5 - 9 + 18 = 4$

Next, we find the cofactor $C_{23}$:

$C_{23} = (-1)^{2+3} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = -(1 \times 3 - 3 \times 3) = -(3 - 9) = 6$

Therefore, the required element is $\dfrac{C_{23}}{|A|} = \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, $C = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$ and $AB = C$, then the inverse of matrix B is
questions.solution:
Given $AB = C$

Taking inverse on both sides, we get $(AB)^{-1} = C^{-1}$

$B^{-1}A^{-1} = C^{-1}$

Multiplying both sides by $A$ on the right, we get $B^{-1} = C^{-1}A$

We have $C = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$

$|C| = 7(6) - 3(0) = 42$

$C^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{42}\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, $B^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{42}\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

$B^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{42}\begin{bmatrix} 18+3 & 6-6 \\ 0-7 & 0+14 \end{bmatrix}$

$B^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{42}\begin{bmatrix} 21 & 0 \\ -7 & 14 \end{bmatrix}$

$B^{-1} = \dfrac{7}{42}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$, then the matrix $A^{-3}$ when $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ is equal to...
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}$

Using the property of rotation matrices, $A^n = \begin{bmatrix} \cos n\theta & -\sin n\theta \\ \sin n\theta & \cos n\theta \end{bmatrix}$ for any integer $n$.

For $n = -3$, we have:

$A^{-3} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(-3\theta) & -\sin(-3\theta) \\ \sin(-3\theta) & \cos(-3\theta) \end{bmatrix}$

Since $\cos(-x) = \cos x$ and $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$, this simplifies to:

$A^{-3} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos 3\theta & \sin 3\theta \\ -\sin 3\theta & \cos 3\theta \end{bmatrix}$

Substituting $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, we get $3\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:

$A^{-3} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} & \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ -\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} & \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{bmatrix}$

$A^{-3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2k-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2k-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2k-1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2k-1 & 1 \\ 1-2k & 0 & k \\ -1 & -k & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ where k is a real number. If $\det(\text{adj} A) + \det(\text{adj} B) = 11^6$, then the value of $k - 5$ is equal to...
questions.solution:
The determinant of the upper triangular matrix $A$ is the product of its diagonal elements:

$|A| = (2k-1)^3$

The matrix $B$ is a skew-symmetric matrix of odd order ($3 \times 3$), so its determinant is zero:

$|B| = 0$

Using the property $|\text{adj} M| = |M|^{n-1}$ for a matrix of order $n$, we have:

$|\text{adj} A| = |A|^2 = ((2k-1)^3)^2 = (2k-1)^6$

$|\text{adj} B| = |B|^2 = 0$

Given $|\text{adj} A| + |\text{adj} B| = 11^6$, we get:

$(2k-1)^6 + 0 = 11^6$

$2k-1 = \pm 11$

$2k = 12 \Rightarrow k = 6$

$2k = -10 \Rightarrow k = -5$

Checking the given options for the value of $k - 5$:

If $k = 6$, $k - 5 = 6 - 5 = 1$

If $k = -5$, $k - 5 = -5 - 5 = -10$

Since $-10$ is not among the options, we take $k = 6$, which gives $1$.

Answer: $1$

questions.q: The element in 1st row and 2nd column of the inverse of the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \\ -3 & 0 & -5 \\ 2 & 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is ...
questions.solution:
Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \\ -3 & 0 & -5 \\ 2 & 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of $A$ is given by:

$|A| = 1(0 - (-25)) - 3(0 - (-10)) - 2(-15 - 0)$

$|A| = 25 - 30 + 30 = 25$

The inverse of matrix $A$ is $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$.

The element in the 1st row and 2nd column of $A^{-1}$ is $\dfrac{1}{|A|} C_{21}$, where $C_{21}$ is the cofactor of the element $a_{21}$ in $A$.

$C_{21} = (-1)^{2+1} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -(0 - (-10)) = -10$

Therefore, the required element is $\dfrac{-10}{25} = -\dfrac{2}{5}$.

questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} \sec\theta & -\tan\theta \\ -\tan\theta & \sec\theta \end{bmatrix}$, $\theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ such that $A + adj\,A = 4I$, then $\theta =$
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} \sec\theta & -\tan\theta \\ -\tan\theta & \sec\theta \end{bmatrix}$

The adjoint of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is $\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$.

$adj\,A = \begin{bmatrix} \sec\theta & \tan\theta \\ \tan\theta & \sec\theta \end{bmatrix}$

$A + adj\,A = \begin{bmatrix} \sec\theta & -\tan\theta \\ -\tan\theta & \sec\theta \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \sec\theta & \tan\theta \\ \tan\theta & \sec\theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2\sec\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 2\sec\theta \end{bmatrix}$

Given $A + adj\,A = 4I$, we have:

$\begin{bmatrix} 2\sec\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 2\sec\theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

$2\sec\theta = 4 \Rightarrow \sec\theta = 2$

Since $\theta \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 3}$, and $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \gamma & -1 & 1 \\ \alpha & 6 & -5 \\ \beta & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}_{3 \times 3}$, then $|\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma| = $ _____ (where $|\cdot|$ denotes the absolute value)
questions.solution:
The determinant of matrix $A$ is:

$|A| = 2(1 \times 3 - 0 \times 1) - 0 + (-1)(5 \times 1 - 1 \times 0) = 6 - 5 = 1$

Since $|A| = 1$, the inverse of $A$ is simply its adjugate matrix, $A^{-1} = \text{adj}(A)$.

The elements $\gamma, \alpha, \beta$ form the first column of $A^{-1}$, which corresponds to the cofactors $C_{11}, C_{12}, C_{13}$ of the first row of matrix $A$.

Calculating these cofactors:

$C_{11} = (1)(3) - (0)(1) = 3 \Rightarrow \gamma = 3$

$C_{12} = -((5)(3) - (0)(0)) = -15 \Rightarrow \alpha = -15$

$C_{13} = (5)(1) - (1)(0) = 5 \Rightarrow \beta = 5$

The product of these values is:

$\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma = (-15) \cdot 5 \cdot 3 = -225$

Taking the absolute value:

$|\alpha \cdot \beta \cdot \gamma| = |-225| = 225$

Answer: $225$

questions.q: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. The Row transformation $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 + 3R_2$ will transform matrix A into
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Applying the row transformation $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 + 3R_2$, the elements of the first row become:

$a_{11} = -5 + 3(2) = 1$

$a_{12} = -3 + 3(1) = 0$

The transformed matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Since all elements above the principal diagonal are zero, it is a lower triangular matrix.

Answer: a lower triangular matrix

questions.q: If $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2i & i^3 \\ i^2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then $A^{-1}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2i & i^3 \\ i^2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Substituting $i^2 = -1$ and $i^3 = -i$, we get:

$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2i & -i \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

The determinant of $A$ is:

$|A| = (2i)(1) - (-i)(-1) = 2i - i = i$

The adjugate of $A$ is:

$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & i \\ 1 & 2i \end{bmatrix}$

The inverse of $A$ is given by $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$

$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{i} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & i \\ 1 & 2i \end{bmatrix}$

Since $\dfrac{1}{i} = -i$, we have:

$A^{-1} = -i \begin{bmatrix} 1 & i \\ 1 & 2i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -i & -i^2 \\ -i & -2i^2 \end{bmatrix}$

Substituting $i^2 = -1$:

$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} -i & 1 \\ -i & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} -i & 1 \\ -i & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ then $A^{-1} - A^2$ is not
questions.solution:
Given $A = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

Calculating $A^2$:

$A^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 1-3 & \sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3} \\ -\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3} & -3+1 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2\sqrt{3} \\ -2\sqrt{3} & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & \sqrt{3} \\ -\sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, finding the determinant of $A$:

$|A| = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 ((-1)(-1) - (-\sqrt{3})(\sqrt{3})) = \dfrac{1}{4} (1 + 3) = 1$

The inverse of $A$ is given by $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A)$:

$A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & \sqrt{3} \\ -\sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix}$

Thus, $A^{-1} - A^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & \sqrt{3} \\ -\sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & \sqrt{3} \\ -\sqrt{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = O$

The result is a null matrix. A null matrix is also a diagonal matrix (all non-diagonal elements are zero) and a scalar matrix (all diagonal elements are equal). However, it is not a unit matrix since its diagonal elements are zero, not $1$.

Answer: a unit matrix

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 4\end{array}\right]$ then $A(I+\operatorname{adj} A)=$
questions.solution:
Given $A(I + \operatorname{adj} A)$, expand to $AI + A(\operatorname{adj} A)$. Since $AI = A$ and $A(\operatorname{adj} A) = |A|I$, the expression simplifies to $A + |A|I$.

Compute the determinant of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$:

$|A| = 1 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 4 \end{vmatrix} - (-2) \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} + 2 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 \end{vmatrix}$

$|A| = 1(8 - 6) + 2(0 - (-9)) + 2(0 - 6) = 2 + 18 - 12 = 8$

Substitute to get $A + 8I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$

Add the matrices element-wise:

$\begin{bmatrix} 9 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 10 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 12 \end{bmatrix}$

This matches option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A$ is a matrix of order 2 and $I$ is the identity matrix of order 2 such that $\mathrm{A}^2-4 \mathrm{~A}+3 \mathrm{I}=0$ then $(\mathrm{A}+3 \mathrm{I})^{-1}=$
questions.solution:
Given the matrix equation $A^2 - 4A + 3I = 0$, we seek the inverse of $A + 3I$.

Let $X = A + 3I$, so that $A = X - 3I$. Substituting into the given equation:

$(X - 3I)^2 - 4(X - 3I) + 3I = 0$

Expanding, since $X$ and $I$ commute:

$X^2 - 6X + 9I - 4X + 12I + 3I = 0$

Combining terms:

$X^2 - 10X + 24I = 0$

Rewriting to isolate $24I$:

$24I = 10X - X^2$

Factoring the right side:

$24I = X(10I - X)$

Multiplying both sides on the right by $X^{-1}$:

$24X^{-1} = 10I - X$

Solving for $X^{-1}$:

$X^{-1} = \frac{1}{24}(10I - X)$

Substituting $X = A + 3I$:

$(A + 3I)^{-1} = \frac{1}{24}(7I - A)$

This matches option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Matrix $A$ is non-singular matrix and $(A-3 I)(A-5 I)=0$, then $\frac{15}{8} A^{-1}=$ _________
questions.solution:
Given a non-singular matrix $A$ satisfying $(A-3I)(A-5I)=0$, expand the product:

$(A-3I)(A-5I)=A^2-8A+15I=0$.

Since $A$ is invertible, multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$:

$A^{-1}(A^2-8A+15I)=A-8I+15A^{-1}=0$.

Rearranging gives $15A^{-1}=8I-A$.

Dividing both sides by 8 yields:

$\frac{15}{8}A^{-1}=I-\frac{1}{8}A$.

This matches option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\mathrm{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}5 a & -\mathrm{b} \\ 3 & 2\end{array}\right]$ and A.adj $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{AA}^{\mathrm{T}}$, then $5 a+\mathrm{b}=$
questions.solution:
Given that $A \cdot \mathrm{adj}(A) = (\det A) I$ and $A \cdot \mathrm{adj}(A) = A A^T$, it follows that $(\det A) I = A A^T$.

For matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 5a & -b \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, the determinant is $\det A = (5a)(2) - (-b)(3) = 10a + 3b$.

Computing $A A^T$ yields:

$A A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 5a & -b \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5a & 3 \\ -b & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 25a^2 + b^2 & 15a - 2b \\ 15a - 2b & 13 \end{bmatrix}$

Equating $(\det A) I = \begin{bmatrix} 10a + 3b & 0 \\ 0 & 10a + 3b \end{bmatrix}$ with $A A^T$ gives the system:

$15a - 2b = 0$

$10a + 3b = 13$

From $15a = 2b$, we have $b = \frac{15}{2}a$. Substituting into the second equation:

$10a + 3\left(\frac{15}{2}a\right) = 13 \Rightarrow 10a + \frac{45}{2}a = 13 \Rightarrow \frac{65}{2}a = 13 \Rightarrow a = \frac{2}{5}$

Then $b = \frac{15}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{5} = 3$.

These values satisfy the diagonal equation $10a + 3b = 25a^2 + b^2 = 13$, confirming consistency.

Therefore, $5a + b = 5\left(\frac{2}{5}\right) + 3 = 2 + 3 = 5$.

Final answer: $\boxed{5}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A=\left[\begin{array}{lll}3 & -3 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{array}\right]_{3 \times 3}$, then $A^{-1}=$
questions.solution:
The determinant of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ evaluates to $\det(A) = 3[(-3)(1) - (4)(-1)] + 3[(2)(1) - (4)(0)] + 4[(2)(-1) - (-3)(0)] = 3(1) + 3(2) + 4(-2) = 1$.

The cofactor matrix is computed as $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$, yielding the adjoint $\operatorname{adj}(A) = C^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$.

Thus, $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)} \operatorname{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$.

Computing $A^2 = A \cdot A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$ and then $A^3 = A^2 \cdot A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & -4 \\ -2 & 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}$ shows that $A^{-1} = A^3$.

The result corresponds to option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right], B=\operatorname{adj} A$ and $C=5 A$, then $\frac{|\operatorname{adj} B|}{|C|}=$
questions.solution:
Calculating the required ratio involves using determinant properties of adjoint matrices and scalar multiplication.

The determinant of matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is $|A| = 1(0 + 3) + 1(0 + 6) + 1(0 - 4) = 3 + 6 - 4 = 5$.

Since $B = \operatorname{adj} A$ and $A$ is $3 \times 3$, the determinant property $|\operatorname{adj} M| = |M|^{n-1}$ gives $|B| = |A|^2 = 25$.

The adjoint of $B$ similarly yields $|\operatorname{adj} B| = |B|^2 = 625$.

For matrix $C = 5A$, the scalar multiplication property $|kM| = k^n|M|$ gives $|C| = 5^3 \cdot 5 = 625$.

$\frac{|\operatorname{adj} B|}{|C|} = \frac{625}{625} = 1$

$\boxed{1}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A$ and $B$ are non-singular matrices of order 2 such that $(\mathrm{AB})^{-1}=\frac{1}{6}\left[\begin{array}{cc}-7 & -3 \\ 2 & 3\end{array}\right]$ and $\mathrm{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{3}\left[\begin{array}{cc}4 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{array}\right]$ then $\mathrm{B}^{-1}=$
questions.solution:
Inverse matrix computation: The inverse of the product $AB$ relates to the inverses of $A$ and $B$ by $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$.

Given $(AB)^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$.

Multiply both sides of $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$ on the right by $A$:

$B^{-1} = (AB)^{-1}A = \left(\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\right)A$

To determine $A$, invert $A^{-1}$. Let $C = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}C$ and $A = 3C^{-1}$.

The determinant of $C$ is $\det(C) = 4 \cdot 0 - 3 \cdot (-1) = 3$.

The adjugate is $\operatorname{adj}(C) = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$, so $C^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$.

Thus, $A = 3 \cdot \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$.

Substitute into the expression for $B^{-1}$:

$B^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-7 & -3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$

$= \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}(-7)(0) + (-3)(1) & (-7)(-3) + (-3)(4) \\ (2)(0) + (3)(1) & (2)(-3) + (3)(4)\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 9 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}$

Factor: $B^{-1} = \frac{3}{6}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$

This corresponds with option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If matrix $A=\frac{1}{11}\left[\begin{array}{rrr}-1 & 7 & -24 \\ 2 & a & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 15\end{array}\right]$ and $A^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{rrr}3 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ b & -1 & c\end{array}\right]$, then the values of $a, b, c$ respectively are ......
questions.solution:
Given the matrices:

$A = \frac{1}{11}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 7 & -24 \\ 2 & a & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 15\end{bmatrix}$

$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ b & -1 & c\end{bmatrix}$

Since $A \times A^{-1} = I$, we compute the product without the scalar factor first:

$\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 7 & -24 \\ 2 & a & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 15\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ b & -1 & c\end{bmatrix} = 11I$

Determine $b$ from the (1,1) entry:

$(-1)(3) + (7)(2) + (-24)(b) = 11 \Rightarrow -3 + 14 - 24b = 11 \Rightarrow -24b = 0 \Rightarrow b = 0$

Determine $a$ from the (2,2) entry:

questions.q: If $A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & \cot \frac{\theta}{2} \\ -\cot \frac{\theta}{2} & 1\end{array}\right]$ then $A^{-1}=$
questions.solution:
Matrix Inverse Computation

The inverse of $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ is given by $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A} \operatorname{adj}(A)$.

For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \cot \frac{\theta}{2} \\ -\cot \frac{\theta}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, the determinant computes as $\det A = 1 \cdot 1 - \left(\cot \frac{\theta}{2}\right)\left(-\cot \frac{\theta}{2}\right) = 1 + \cot^2 \frac{\theta}{2}$.

Using the identity $1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x$, this simplifies to $\det A = \csc^2 \frac{\theta}{2}$.

The adjugate matrix is $\operatorname{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\cot \frac{\theta}{2} \\ \cot \frac{\theta}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, which equals $A^T$.

Combining these gives $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\csc^2 \frac{\theta}{2}} A^T = \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2} A^T$.

Applying the half-angle identity $\sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$ yields $\sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{2}$, so $A^{-1} = \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{2} A^T$.

This matches option D.

questions.solution:
A non-singular matrix $A$ of order $n$ with $|A|=k$ satisfies the fundamental relationship $\operatorname{adj} A = |A| A^{-1} = k A^{-1}$.

The inverse of $\operatorname{adj} A$ is then given by $(\operatorname{adj} A)^{-1} = (k A^{-1})^{-1} = \frac{1}{k} (A^{-1})^{-1} = \frac{1}{k} A$.

This result corresponds to option A, $\frac{A}{k}$.

questions.solution:
Adjoint element $\left(\text{adj} A\right)_{23}$ corresponds to the cofactor $C_{32}$ of matrix $A$.

Matrix $A$ with elements $a_{ij} = 2i + j$ for $i,j = 1,2,3$ yields:

$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 5 & 6 & 7 \\ 7 & 8 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$

Cofactor $C_{32} = (-1)^{3+2} M_{32} = -M_{32}$, where $M_{32}$ is the determinant of the submatrix after removing row 3 and column 2:

$M_{32} = \det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 5 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = 3 \times 7 - 5 \times 5 = 21 - 25 = -4$

Thus, $C_{32} = -(-4) = 4$, and $\left(\text{adj} A\right)_{23} = 4$. The final answer is $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.q: If $\mathrm{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & \tan x \\ -\tan x & 1\end{array}\right]$, then $\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{A}^{-1}=$
questions.solution:
The transpose of $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \tan x \\ -\tan x & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ is $A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tan x \\ \tan x & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

The determinant evaluates to $|A| = (1)(1) - (\tan x)(-\tan x) = 1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x$, using the trigonometric identity.

The adjugate matrix is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tan x \\ \tan x & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, leading to the inverse:

$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\sec^2 x} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tan x \\ \tan x & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos^2 x & -\sin x \cos x \\ \sin x \cos x & \cos^2 x \end{bmatrix}$

Multiplying matrices:

$A^T A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tan x \\ \tan x & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \cos^2 x & -\sin x \cos x \\ \sin x \cos x & \cos^2 x \end{bmatrix}$

The product yields $\begin{bmatrix} \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x & -2\sin x \cos x \\ 2\sin x \cos x & \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x \end{bmatrix}$

Applying double-angle identities, this simplifies to $\begin{bmatrix} \cos 2x & -\sin 2x \\ \sin 2x & \cos 2x \end{bmatrix}$

This result corresponds to option B.

questions.q: If $\mathrm{A}=\left[\begin{array}{rr}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4\end{array}\right]$ and $\mathrm{A}^{-1}=\alpha \mathrm{I}+\beta \mathrm{A}\alpha, \beta \in \mathrm{R}$ where I is the identity matrix of order 2 , then $4(\alpha+\beta)=$
questions.solution:
The inverse matrix $\mathrm{A}^{-1}$ is expressed as $\mathrm{A}^{-1} = \alpha\mathrm{I} + \beta\mathrm{A}$. One approach begins by computing $\mathrm{A}^{-1}$ directly for the given matrix.

The determinant is $\det(\mathrm{A}) = (1)(4) - (2)(-1) = 6$. Constructing the adjugate yields $\left[\begin{array}{rr}4 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{array}\right]$, so

$\mathrm{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\left[\begin{array}{rr}4 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr}\frac{2}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{6}\end{array}\right]$.

Equating this to $\alpha\mathrm{I} + \beta\mathrm{A} = \left[\begin{array}{rr}\alpha+\beta & 2\beta \\ -\beta & \alpha+4\beta\end{array}\right]$, the elements yield the system

$\alpha + \beta = \frac{2}{3}$
$2\beta = -\frac{1}{3}$

Solving gives $\beta = -\frac{1}{6}$ and thus $\alpha = \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$.

A more elegant method uses the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 6 = 0$, so $\mathrm{A}^2 - 5\mathrm{A} + 6\mathrm{I} = \mathbf{0}$. Multiplying by $\mathrm{A}^{-1}$ gives

$\mathrm{A} - 5\mathrm{I} + 6\mathrm{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{0}$
$\mathrm{A}^{-1} = \frac{5}{6}\mathrm{I} - \frac{1}{6}\mathrm{A}$

Matching coefficients confirms $\alpha = \frac{5}{6}$ and $\beta = -\frac{1}{6}$.

Evaluating the required expression gives $4(\alpha + \beta) = 4\left(\frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{6}\right) = 4\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) = \frac{8}{3}$.

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned}|A| & =\left|\begin{array}{cc}1 & \tan x \\ -\tan x & 1\end{array}\right| \\ & =1+\tan ^2 x \neq 0\end{aligned} \\ & \text { If } A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}a & b \\ c & d\end{array}\right] \text { and ad }-b c \neq 0, \\ & \text { then } A^{-1}=\frac{1}{(a d-b c)}\left[\begin{array}{cc}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \mathrm{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1+\tan ^2 x}\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & -\tan x \\ \tan x & 1\end{array}\right] \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{A}^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & -\tan x \\ \tan x & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{1+\tan ^2 x} & \frac{-\tan x}{1+\tan ^2 x} \\ \frac{\tan x}{1+\tan ^2 x} & \frac{1}{1+\tan ^2 x}\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}\frac{1-\tan ^2 x}{1+\tan ^2 x} & \frac{-2 \tan x}{1+\tan ^2 x} \\ \frac{2 \tan x}{1+\tan ^2 x} & \frac{1-\tan ^2 x}{1+\tan ^2 x}\end{array}\right] \\ & =\left[\begin{array}{ll}\cos 2 x & -\sin 2 x \\ \sin 2 x & \cos 2 x\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{a}_{21}=-1, \mathrm{a}_{22}=1, \mathrm{a}_{23}=2 \\ & \mathrm{~A}_{21}=(-1)^{2+1}\left|\begin{array}{ll}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{array}\right|=(-1)(2)=-2 \\ & \mathrm{~A}_{22}=(-1)^{2+2}\left|\begin{array}{ll}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{array}\right|=1(1)=1 \\ & \quad \mathrm{~A}_{23}=(-1)^{2+3}\left|\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{array}\right|=(-1)(0)=0 \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{a}_{21} \mathrm{~A}_{21}+\mathrm{a}_{22} \mathrm{~A}_{22}+\mathrm{a}_{23} \mathrm{~A}_{23}=(-1)(-2)+1(1)+2(0) \\ &=3\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 a & -3 b \\ 3 & 2\end{array}\right] \\ & A \cdot \operatorname{adj} A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 a & -3 b \\ 3 & 2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 & 3 b \\ -3 & 2 a\end{array}\right] \\ & =\left[\begin{array}{cc}4 a+9 b & 0 \\ 0 & 9 b+4 a\end{array}\right] \\ & A \cdot A^T=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 a & -3 b \\ 3 & 2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 a & 3 \\ -3 b & 2\end{array}\right] \\ & =\left[\begin{array}{cc}4 a^2+9 b^2 & 6 a-6 b \\ 6 a-6 b & 13\end{array}\right] \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{A} \cdot \operatorname{adj} \mathrm{A}=\mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \\ & \Rightarrow\left[\begin{array}{cc}4 a+9 b & 0 \\ 0 & 4 a+9 b\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}4 a^2+9 b^2 & 6 a-6 b \\ 6 a-6 b & 13\end{array}\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{b} \text { and } 4 \mathrm{a}+9 \mathrm{~b}=13 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{b}=1 \\ & \Rightarrow 2 a+3 b=5 \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ -5 & 1\end{array}\right] \\ \therefore \quad & \mathrm{A} \mid=11 \\ & \mathrm{~A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{~A}|}\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{array}\right]=\frac{1}{11}\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{array}\right] \\ & \mathrm{A}^{-1}=x \mathrm{~A}+y \mathrm{I}, \text { we get } \\ & {\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{11} & \frac{-2}{11} \\ \frac{5}{11} & \frac{1}{11}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}x & 2 x \\ -5 x & x\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}{ll}y & 0 \\ 0 & y\end{array}\right] }\end{aligned}\begin{array}{ll}\therefore & {\left[\begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{11} & \frac{-2}{11} \\ \frac{5}{11} & \frac{1}{11}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{cc}x+y & 2 x \\ -5 x & x+y\end{array}\right]} \\ \Rightarrow & x=\frac{-1}{11} \text { and } y=\frac{2}{11} \\ \therefore & 2 x+3 y=2\left(\frac{-1}{11}\right)+3\left(\frac{2}{11}\right)=\frac{4}{11}\end{array}$
